script: Roy and Ryan Siders kept destroying their coolers. The brothers were avid fishermen and hunters in Texas who spent days in the field with cheap plastic coolers that cracked, let ice melt in hours, and fell apart under real use. Every cooler on the market was built for a backyard barbecue, not for two days on a boat in August heat. In 2006, they decided to build one themselves. They went to the same rotomolding factories that made commercial marine equipment and had a cooler built to those specs. Walls thick enough to hold ice for days, a lid that sealed properly, and latches that didn't snap off. It weighed significantly more than anything else on the market and cost significantly more, too. Outdoor retailers passed. So the brothers sold direct, mostly at trade shows and to guides and outfitters who immediately understood what they were looking at. Word spread through hunting and fishing communities before it reached anyone else. By the time mainstream consumers discovered Yeti, it had already become the default cooler among people who used coolers seriously. The brand extended into drinkware, bags, and soft coolers. In 2018, Yeti went public at a valuation of $1.7 billion.
